nameStory: The 'baskettail' name comes from the female's unique egg-laying behavior - she carries her eggs in a sticky mass at the tip of her abdomen that looks like a tiny basket! This distinctive 'basket' of eggs is dropped into the water all at once, making these dragonflies easy to spot during their reproductive activities.
description: The Common Baskettail is a medium-sized dragonfly with a sturdy build and distinctively patterned wings. Adults typically measure about 2-3 inches in length with clear wings marked by dark brown spots near the bases. Their bodies are generally dark brown to black with metallic green highlights that shimmer in sunlight. As members of the emerald dragonfly family, they're strong fliers often seen patrolling over ponds and slow streams.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive dark brown triangular spots at the base of all four wings - these feel papery and create a unique 'stained glass' effect when held up to light

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Dark brown to blackish body with bright metallic green sheen on the thorax that catches sunlight like polished metal

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with steady, deliberate wingbeats in regular patrol routes over water, often hovering briefly before darting to a new position

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a robust, chunky appearance - feels substantial if gently handled, unlike more delicate damselflies

idTips.label: Eye Position
idTips.description: Large compound eyes that nearly touch at the top of the head, giving excellent all-around vision

habitat: Common Baskettails prefer slow-moving or still waters including ponds, lakes, marshes, and sluggish streams throughout New England's lowlands and mid-elevations. They're often found around areas with emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges where females can easily deposit their egg masses. Look for them near permanent water bodies surrounded by mixed forests or open meadows.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with newly transformed individuals often seen resting on vegetation near water while their wings harden and bodies mature.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August when adults are most visible patrolling territories, mating, and females can be spotted carrying distinctive egg masses at their abdomen tips.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly by September, though stragglers may be seen into early October during warm spells before frost kills the adults.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - young nymphs overwinter underwater in mud and debris, developing slowly until ready to emerge the following spring.

funFact: Female Common Baskettails can carry up to 2,000 eggs in their abdominal 'basket' - and they've been observed taste-testing potential egg-laying sites by dipping their abdomen in the water before deciding if the chemistry is right for their babies!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other baskettail species, but the Common Baskettail's wing spots are more triangular and clearly defined compared to the rounder, hazier spots of Prince Baskettails. Memory trick: 'Common' baskettails have 'clean' triangular wing marks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'emerald' dragonflies, most family members including Common Baskettails appear quite dark in normal light - the emerald green coloration only becomes obvious in bright sunlight or when viewed at certain angles, which can confuse beginning dragonfly watchers expecting bright green insects.
compareHints: Among New England baskettails, the Common Baskettail is distinguished by its smaller size compared to Prince Baskettails and clearer wing markings than Beaverpond Baskettails. The triangular basal wing spots are more sharply defined than in other baskettail species, and it lacks the distinctive yellow abdominal markings found on Spiny Baskettails.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the baskettails, the Beaverpond Baskettail is most closely tied to beaver-modified habitats, while the Common Baskettail prefers larger lakes and rivers, and the Prince Baskettail favors flowing streams.
Prince Baskettail is the largest of New England's baskettails and the only one with such prominent yellow markings on a brown body.
Among New England baskettails, the Mantled Baskettail is the only one with prominent dark shoulder patches, making it relatively easy to distinguish.
